Martin Kray had listened to Elias Prine describe the blank chambers in his mind and found no damage there.

“You remember how to speak, how to dress, how to get home,” Martin had said across the insurance desk. “You forget only what hurts.”

Prine’s wife was diabetic. According to the file, she had tested him one evening by asking for her injection, then asking again, then again. Each time he obeyed. Each time he forgot. She died with the needle near her hand and Prine kneeling beside her, unable to remember killing her.

Martin ruled the amnesia psychosomatic and denied the claim.

Later, intruders broke into Martin’s house and attacked him and his wife in their bathroom. Martin killed one against the tiles. The other struck him across the head and escaped. When Martin woke, his wife was dead, and his mind no longer carried one moment into the next.

He began manufacturing memory.

Instant photographs showed faces, rooms, objects. Notes in his own handwriting told him whom to trust. Tattoos made facts harder to lose. The second attacker was a man known only by the initials R.M., and Martin arranged his life around hunting him.

A plainclothes officer named Roy helped him. Nearly a year before the last days of the hunt, Roy found the real attacker and led Martin to him. Martin killed the man who had murdered his wife.

Within minutes, the vengeance was gone.

In a motel room he could not remember renting, Martin sat on the bed and spoke into the telephone. An anonymous caller listened while Martin narrated the Prine case: Elias, his diabetic wife, the repeated injections, the overdose, the convenient forgetting.

The story felt important, though Martin could not say why.

He drove to a field with his wife’s hairbrush and her books piled on the passenger seat. He burned them beneath an empty sky. Smoke took her hair from the bristles and curled pages into ash. He tried to grieve, but grief required continuity. Each time his eyes wandered, the fire became a mystery again.

The caller gave him a name and a location.

Gil Marsh. Drug dealer. The man Martin wanted.

Martin found Gil in the basement of a derelict building. He beat him against damp concrete, wrapped an arm around his throat and held on until the struggling stopped. Then he photographed the body.

Gil’s last breath shaped a word.

“Elias.”

Martin stared at him, waiting for the name to mean something. It did not. He removed Gil’s suit, dressed himself in it, took the dead man’s sports car and went outside.

Roy arrived furious.

“Gil was innocent,” he said. “You already killed the man who did it. I helped you.

Danny Roarke rehearsed the lie until it acquired the worn edges of truth.

“It was a public toilet,” Pruitt said. “Not an alley.”

“Public toilet.”

“And the dealer had the package taped under the cistern.”

Danny began again. He described the stink of disinfectant, the uniformed officers entering while he stood at the urinal with drugs in his pocket, the dog sniffing his shoes. Pruitt interrupted whenever he rushed or embellished. By midnight, Danny no longer recited it. He remembered it.

He told the story days later to Bram, Bram’s son Cal, and a narrow-eyed man called Mr. Ash. They watched for cracks, but Danny gave them sweat, pauses, even a laugh in the right place.

Bram nodded. “You’ll do. From now on, you’re Mr. Elm.”

That same week Ren Vasco walked out of prison carrying everything he owned in a paper sack. He went straight to Bram and Cal.

“I gave you years,” Ren said. “Never opened my mouth.”

Bram embraced him. Cal promised they had not forgotten.

Before the job, they ate breakfast in a crowded diner. A pop song played overhead, and the table divided over whether it was about love, betrayal, or sex. Then Mr. Birch refused to leave a tip.

“Waitresses get paid,” Birch said.

“Barely,” Ash replied.

Bram ended the argument by passing out aliases. Cedar accepted his. Ash shrugged at his. Danny already knew his.

“Mr. Birch?” Ren said. “Why am I Mr. Birch? Birch sounds weak.”

“You’re Birch because I said so,” Bram told him.

The robbery collapsed in less than a minute.

An alarm screamed. Police appeared from both ends of the street. Civilians scattered as glass burst across the pavement. Ash dragged Elm into the getaway car and fired through the rear window, forcing a path through the cruisers.

When the car crashed, they ran. Elm yanked open the door of a stopped sedan and pointed his pistol at the driver. The terrified man fumbled beneath his coat and fired. The bullet struck Elm in the stomach. Elm shot him dead before he understood he had pulled the trigger.

Ash took the wheel. Elm screamed all the way to the warehouse.

“You’re not dying,” Ash said, cradling him on the concrete floor. “Hear me? You are not dying.”

Birch arrived wild-eyed and bloody. He said the police had been waiting, that the entire job had been a setup, that one of them was an informer. Before entering, he hid the diamonds outside the building, beneath a heap of scrap.

Then Cedar strolled in as if returning from lunch. He opened his boot and hauled out a bound patrolman named Doyle.

When the others left to fetch Bram, Cedar remained with Doyle and the fading Elm. An old song came over the radio. Cedar danced, loose and smiling, circling the chair. He drew a knife, sliced off Doyle’s ear, then splashed petrol over him.

From the floor, Elm raised his gun.

The shot killed Cedar instantly.

Elm crawled to Doyle and whispered, “I’m a cop. Police are outside, waiting for Bram. Just hold on.”

Cal returned first.

Years before blood and bad luck tangled the city together, a prisoner of war came home carrying a secret. He found a young boy named Denny and placed a gold watch in his hand. The boy’s father had hidden it through years of captivity, refusing to let guards or hunger take it. He had died before he could return, so his comrade had brought it home.

Denny never forgot.

Much later, hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city discussing foreign drug laws, the names of fast food overseas, and the strange customs people treated as ordinary. Outside a target’s flat, their conversation turned to foot massages. Rollo thought one could be intimate enough to justify murder. Marcus considered that absurd.

Inside, a frightened young man named Tobin waited with his friends. He had double-crossed their employer, Otis, and lost a valuable briefcase. Marcus recited scripture with the solemnity of a preacher, then he and Rollo opened fire. They recovered the case.

A fourth man burst from the bathroom and emptied a revolver at them. Every bullet missed.

Marcus stared at the holes in the wall. “Divine intervention,” he said.

Rollo laughed it off. Later, in the car, his pistol discharged by accident and blew off the head of their passenger, Del.

Marcus drove the blood-soaked vehicle to the home of his friend Warren. A brisk fixer arrived, ordered the car scrubbed, the remains concealed, and the two hitmen washed. Soon they were dressed in borrowed clothes that made them look ridiculous but clean.

That morning, in a coffee shop, a pair of small-time robbers looked around and decided diners were easier prey than banks or liquor stores. They stood, drew weapons, and began collecting wallets.

Marcus, still carrying Otis’s briefcase, refused to surrender it. Calmly, he took control of the confrontation. He talked the robber down, gave him his own wallet, and let the couple leave alive. To Marcus, the morning had confirmed what the bullets had already told him: he was being offered a way out.

He and Rollo delivered the briefcase to Otis’s bar. There, Otis was paying an ageing boxer named Denny to fall in the fifth round of an upcoming fight.

Rollo later visited his dealer, Kip, bought heroin, and shot up before taking Otis’s wife Nadia out for the evening. At a themed diner, they entered a dance contest and won. Back home, Nadia found Rollo’s heroin, mistook it for something else, and snorted it. She collapsed.

Panicked, Rollo carried her to Kip’s house. On the living-room floor, amid shouting and confusion, they drove an adrenaline needle into her heart. Nadia jolted awake with a gasp.

The next night, Denny ignored his arrangement with Otis. He won the fight and killed his opponent in the ring. Knowing Otis would hunt him, he escaped in a taxi and hid at a motel with his girlfriend, Marielle.

Then he learned she had forgotten his father’s gold watch.

Denny returned alone to his flat. The watch was there. So was a submachine gun on the kitchen counter. Hearing someone in the bathroom, Denny picked it up. Rollo emerged, and Denny shot him dead.

Leaving the building, Denny encountered Otis in the street. Recognition flashed between them. A chase became a collision, and both men crashed hard. Before either could settle their feud, the pawnshop owner dragged them into a basement and chained them.

Denny broke free. He could have escaped, but when he heard Otis being raped by one of their captors, he stopped. Upstairs, weapons hung along the walls. Denny chose a sword.

He returned to the basement and cut down the attackers. Bloodied and furious, Otis told him they were square, on one condition: Denny must leave the city forever.

Denny needed no persuasion. He collected Marielle, placed her behind him on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop, and rode away with the gold watch secure against his body and the city shrinking behind them.

In a mining boarding house out west, Emmett Rusk’s mother signed her son away to Barrow, the banker. A lodger had defaulted on his bill and left behind a mine deed; the worthless paper proved valuable, making the Rusks rich overnight. Barrow would manage the fortune and educate the boy. Emmett’s mother wept as she signed. Emmett drove his sled hard into Barrow’s stomach, but they took him east anyway, away from his parents and the snowbound yard.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett assumed control of his wealth. Barrow spread before him the inventory of mines, railroads, timberlands, ships and factories.

“I want the Clarion,” Emmett said.

“The failing newspaper?”

“That’s the one.”

He moved into the Clarion’s offices as if invading a country, installing the practical Marsh as manager and his old friend Devlin among the editors. On the first morning, the front page carried Emmett’s signed declaration: the Clarion would tell the truth, defend the weak and answer to no party or purse.

He celebrated those principles by hiring the rival paper’s entire staff. A brass band played through the newsroom while a chorus line kicked between the desks and champagne soaked the copy.

After a buying trip abroad, Emmett returned engaged to Adele, the governor’s niece. Their marriage began in public brilliance and cooled at the breakfast table. Morning after morning they sat at opposite ends, hidden behind separate newspapers. Pages turned. Cups touched saucers. Soon silence was the only thing they shared.

Emmett met Nora Kell on a wet street after a carriage splashed mud across his coat. She laughed before recognizing him. Nora was a shopgirl with plain rooms and an unguarded smile, and he began visiting her there in secret.

When Emmett ran for governor, party boss Halloran discovered the affair. In the middle of the campaign he brought Adele to Nora’s rooms and offered Emmett a choice: withdraw or be exposed.

“Print it,” Emmett said.

He lost the election. Devlin asked for transfer to another city, and Adele’s long silence hardened into the end of their marriage.

Emmett married Nora. Because he loved her voice when she sang carelessly, he decided the world must call it great. Teachers, conductors and theaters yielded to his money. Nora protested that she had no operatic voice. Emmett called that fear.

Her debut was a humiliation. The audience tittered, then laughed. That night Devlin, drunk and bitter, began a savage review. Emmett found him slumped over the unfinished copy. He finished the review himself, printed it, and fired Devlin.

Rather than sing again, Nora swallowed poison. Emmett sat beside her bed and, for once, surrendered.

“You can stop,” he told her.

He shut her away afterward in Silvermount, the half-finished palace he had built above the world. Crates crowded unfinished galleries; statues stood beneath sheets. In the vast empty hall, Nora worked jigsaw puzzles while her pieces clicked into place and her life did not.

They tried a beach picnic, joyless beneath a pale sky. A quarrel followed them home. Nora packed and left.

Emmett entered her bedroom and wrecked it—furniture, bottles, mirrors, curtains—until he found a glass snow globe. Snow drifted around a tiny winter house.

“Bluebell,” he murmured.

He carried it through corridors lined with endless mirrors, each reflection bearing the same old man and the same small world.

Alone at Silvermount, Emmett Rusk died with “Bluebell” on his lips. The globe slipped from his hand and shattered on the floor.

A newsreel obituary recounted the public life: the newspaper empire, the political crusades, the election defeat, the opera house, the palace, the scandals and acquisitions. It ended by admitting that no one could explain his final word.

The reporter Nash was assigned to discover what it meant. At a seaside nightclub, Nora—drunk, performing beneath tired lights—turned him away. Nash read Barrow’s memoir, then interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora again, and Colm, the old butler. Each offered an Emmett assembled from different pieces: tyrant, friend, fraud, wounded child, lonely king.

At last Nash closed his notebook. No single word, he decided, could explain a life.

At Silvermount, workmen fed Emmett’s possessions into a furnace. Among the discarded relics was an old sled. None noticed the name painted across it before their shovels lifted it into the fire.

Bluebell.

They met at a beach party in a seaside town where the railway ended. The wind had driven everyone close to the fire, but Ivy wandered away, and Tobias followed her along the black shore. They found an empty house with salt-filmed windows and broke in through a side door. In the bare rooms, they pretended it belonged to them. Ivy danced in the kitchen. Tobias watched her and felt his life divide into before and after.

For two years they accumulated a private world: lying on the frozen river while cracks boomed beneath the ice; sharing noodles at midnight, steam clouding Ivy’s face; kissing at the drive-in while an old monster destroyed a cardboard city onscreen.

Then love turned forensic. Tobias counted Ivy’s drinks. Ivy counted the silences in which he withheld himself. She accused him of standing outside their life, observing. He accused her of drowning every difficult feeling before it could speak.

One night she came home drunk, having dented his car. Their shouting shook the walls.

“You don’t love me,” she said. “You manage me.”

“You make loving you impossible.”

She stared at him until the fury left her face. Then she walked out and did not come back.

Ivy went to a clinic and paid to have every trace of Tobias removed from her memory.

He learned this at the bookshop. She stood behind the counter, laughing with a young man named Peck. When Tobias approached, Ivy gave him the polite, guarded smile reserved for strangers. Then she turned back to Peck and touched his sleeve.

Nina and Grady showed Tobias the clinic’s form letter, clinical condolences confirming the procedure. He carried it to Dr. Hallam, the director, and demanded the same treatment.

At Hallam’s instruction, Tobias boxed everything attached to Ivy: photographs, ticket stubs, a chipped bowl from the noodle house, a drive-in receipt, a scarf smelling faintly of winter. The objects would map the memories.

That night, technicians Dell and Peck installed their equipment in Tobias’s flat. Sensors clung to his scalp. As Tobias sank under, Peck quietly pocketed the mementos, intending to use them to charm Ivy with details stolen from her forgotten life.

Inside his head, Tobias remained awake.

The erasure began with the freshest wounds. Ivy vanished from the night of the dented car, then from the argument before it, then another. Rooms collapsed after she disappeared from them. Accusations lost their targets. Broken glasses reassembled into nothing.

But when the machine reached the memories he loved—the drive-in, the noodle house, the frozen river—Tobias panicked.

“No,” he told Ivy inside the dream. “We have to hide.”

He dragged her into childhood rooms she had never entered, tucked her beneath his grandmother’s table, pushed her through school corridors predating their meeting. Each refuge buckled as the memory map went off the rails.

In the waking flat, Dell and Rosa, the clinic receptionist, got high on Tobias’s bed and stopped watching the monitors. Alarms multiplied unnoticed.

Dr. Hallam arrived to repair the map. Rosa, reckless and aching, kissed him. His wife appeared behind him and told Rosa the truth: Rosa had already had an affair with Hallam. She had already begged to forget it. The clinic had erased her, too.

Within Tobias, only the empty house remained. Moonlight lay across the floorboards. Ivy stood in the bare kitchen where she had once danced.

“We’re running out of places,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want to lose you.”

“You already did.” She touched his face. “Meet me at the beach.”

The house dissolved around them. They said goodbye as the sea rushed through the walls.

Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed.

He dressed for work, reached the station, then stopped. An impulse without a name pulled him onto the coastal train. At the end of the line, he walked over frozen sand and saw a woman alone by the water.

Ivy looked at him. Something in both of them hesitated.

They spoke. They walked. By afternoon they were driving back to the city together, laughing too easily. Outside her building, Ivy invited him up.

Meanwhile, Rosa quit the clinic. She mailed every patient their files and session tapes.

Tobias’s package arrived at Ivy’s flat. They listened to their own recorded voices describing each other with exhausted cruelty. Tobias heard himself call her a drunk. Ivy heard herself call him hollow. The new tenderness between them seemed suddenly fraudulent.

Ivy ran.

Tobias remained by the tape player until she returned, breathless and frightened.

“We’ll do all of that again,” she said.

“Probably.”

“I’ll get bored. You’ll shut down.”

“Yes.”

She waited for him to deny it.

Instead, Tobias said, “I still want to try.”

Ivy looked toward the window, as if listening for a distant sea.

“Okay,” she said. “Then try.”

“You don’t love me,” she said. “You manage me.”

“You make loving you impossible.”

She stared at him until the fury left her face. Then she walked out and did not come back.

He learned this at the bookshop. She stood behind the counter, laughing with a young man named Peck. When Tobias approached, Ivy gave him the polite, guarded smile reserved for strangers. Then she turned back to Peck and touched his sleeve.

Nina and Grady showed Tobias the clinic’s form letter, clinical condolences confirming the procedure. He carried it to Dr. Hallam, the director, and demanded the same treatment.

At Hallam’s instruction, Tobias boxed everything attached to Ivy: photographs, ticket stubs, a chipped bowl from the noodle house, a drive-in receipt, a scarf smelling faintly of winter. The objects would map the memories.

That night, technicians Dell and Peck installed their equipment in Tobias’s flat. Sensors clung to his scalp. As Tobias sank under, Peck quietly pocketed the mementos, intending to use them to charm Ivy with details stolen from her forgotten life.

Inside his head, Tobias remained awake.

The erasure began with the freshest wounds. Ivy vanished from the night of the dented car, then from the argument before it, then another. Rooms collapsed after she disappeared from them. Accusations lost their targets. Broken glasses reassembled into nothing.

But when the machine reached the memories he loved—the drive-in, the noodle house, the frozen river—Tobias panicked.

“No,” he told Ivy inside the dream. “We have to hide.”

He dragged her into childhood rooms she had never entered, tucked her beneath his grandmother’s table, pushed her through school corridors predating their meeting. Each refuge buckled as the memory map went off the rails.

In the waking flat, Dell and Rosa, the clinic receptionist, got high on Tobias’s bed and stopped watching the monitors. Alarms multiplied unnoticed.

Dr. Hallam arrived to repair the map. Rosa, reckless and aching, kissed him. His wife appeared behind him and told Rosa the truth: Rosa had already had an affair with Hallam. She had already begged to forget it. The clinic had erased her, too.

Within Tobias, only the empty house remained. Moonlight lay across the floorboards. Ivy stood in the bare kitchen where she had once danced.

“We’re running out of places,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want to lose you.”

“You already did.” She touched his face. “Meet me at the beach.”

The house dissolved around them. They said goodbye as the sea rushed through the walls.

Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed.

He dressed for work, reached the station, then stopped. An impulse without a name pulled him onto the coastal train. At the end of the line, he walked over frozen sand and saw a woman alone by the water.

Ivy looked at him. Something in both of them hesitated.

They spoke. They walked. By afternoon they were driving back to the city together, laughing too easily. Outside her building, Ivy invited him up.

Meanwhile, Rosa quit the clinic. She mailed every patient their files and session tapes.

Tobias’s package arrived at Ivy’s flat. They listened to their own recorded voices describing each other with exhausted cruelty. Tobias heard himself call her a drunk. Ivy heard herself call him hollow. The new tenderness between them seemed suddenly fraudulent.

Ivy ran.

Tobias remained by the tape player until she returned, breathless and frightened.

“We’ll do all of that again,” she said.

“Probably.”

“I’ll get bored. You’ll shut down.”

“Yes.”

She waited for him to deny it.

Instead, Tobias said, “I still want to try.”

Ivy looked toward the window, as if listening for a distant sea.

“Okay,” she said. “Then try.”

The gun dealer laid the handgun on the glass counter and made Nadir repeat himself twice.

“Bullets,” Nadir said, tightening his jaw.

“Boo-lets,” the dealer mimicked, grinning.

Sahar touched her father’s sleeve before anger carried him somewhere dangerous. While Nadir filled out the forms, she quietly chose the ammunition.

That same night, outside a restaurant bright with linen and glass, Trey and Kwame pulled prosecutor Halstead from his car. They drove away laughing, Halstead’s keys still warm in the ignition.

Across town, Officer Boyle stopped Clay and Renee Hobart. He ordered them out, pressed Renee against the vehicle, and groped her under the pretense of searching her. Clay watched, rigid with humiliation, while Boyle’s partner, Voss, stood nearby and said nothing. Boyle finally sent them off with a warning.

At the station, Voss went to their commander.

“I want another patrol car.”

“Problem with the one you’ve got?”

“The car is fine,” Voss said. “I’m done riding with a racist.”

Mateo arrived at the Halsteads’ home to replace their locks. Paula Halstead watched him from the hallway, speaking loudly enough for him to hear.

“He looks like a gang member. He’ll sell copies of our keys.”

Mateo finished the job without answering. His next call was Nadir’s shop. After fitting the new lock, he showed Nadir the splintered frame.

“The lock won’t matter if you don’t replace the door.”

Nadir heard only another man trying to take his money. “You think I am fool? This is con.”

Later, Boyle sat across from Delia Frank at the health insurance office, stripped of swagger. His father was sick; the prescribed treatment might help.

“The policy won’t cover it,” Delia said.

“He’ll die.”

“I’m sorry.”

Boyle stared at her as if refusal were a violence she had invented.

Overnight, thieves smashed through Nadir’s weakened door. They looted the shop and painted hatred across the walls. The insurer denied his claim because he had ignored the locksmith’s warning. Nadir stood amid broken bottles and ruined shelves, thinking of Mateo.

Then Renee Hobart’s car overturned and caught fire.

She hung upside down, trapped by her seat belt, flames crawling toward her. Boyle recognized her. She recognized him too, and terror sharpened into horror. He crawled into the wreck anyway, glass cutting his arms, and dragged her free seconds before the car bloomed into fire.

Trey and Kwame, meanwhile, struck a shopkeeper named Pham with their car. They panicked, lifted his bleeding body into the vehicle, and dumped him outside a hospital before speeding away.

Clay later found two men trying to steal his own car. Police arrived to see him wrestling for control and raised their weapons. Voss stepped between their certainty and Clay’s death.

“Hold your fire,” he shouted. “That’s his car.”

Trey escaped into the passenger seat, and Clay, seized by fury, drove him away from the police at reckless speed. Then he braked, hauled Trey out, and left him in the road.

Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with the handgun. When Mateo appeared, Nadir raised it. At that instant, little Rosie ran from the house and leaped into her father’s arms.

Nadir fired.

Mateo clutched his daughter. Rosie blinked, untouched. The report vanished into silence, leaving no blood behind. Sahar had bought blanks.

“My angel,” Nadir whispered, believing the child had stopped death itself.

Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking along a dark road. Unease filled the patrol car. When Kwame reached into his pocket, Voss misread the movement and shot him. Afterward, he set fire to the car and watched evidence turn to flame.

Detective Isaiah Reece was called to a body dumped by the roadside. He pulled back the covering and found his brother.

Their mother received the news without tears. “You never even went to look for him,” she told Isaiah. “Not once.”

In the Halstead house, Paula fell down the stairs. Her housekeeper, Alba, found her crumpled at the bottom.

“You’re the only friend I have,” Paula said, clutching her hand.

Trey discovered Pham’s van at the docks, packed with trafficked migrants meant to be sold. He opened the doors instead. Men, women, and children spilled into the cold night and scattered toward uncertain freedom.

Then the first snow of the year began. It softened roofs, windshields, bloodstains, ash. At an intersection, one car struck another. Doors flew open. Drivers stepped into the street, shouting blame, while snow gathered silently on their shoulders.

For months, I survived by borrowing other people’s grief.

Insomnia had hollowed me out. By day I investigated product recalls, measuring the price of crushed bodies against the cost of repairs. By night I stared at the ceiling. Then I found the support groups. Parasites. Blood disorders. Failing organs. I sat among the dying, accepted their arms around me, and cried until I could finally sleep.

Then Ada Vey appeared.

She attended everything, though she was no sicker than I was. Her cigarette smoke clung to her coat; her eyes dared me to expose her. Seeing my own fraud reflected in hers sealed the tears inside me. Sleep vanished again.

On a business flight, I met Rex Marrow, a soap salesman with a grin sharp enough to cut glass. He talked about fat, purity, and the hidden usefulness of waste. When we landed, I pocketed his card.

I needed it sooner than expected. My flat exploded while I was away, reducing every carefully catalogued chair, lamp, and coordinated plate to black fragments. With nowhere else to go, I called Rex.

He took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, where rain came through the roof and the pipes coughed rust. That first night, outside a bar, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could.

I did.

He laughed, struck back, and soon we were rolling across the car park, bleeding and exhilarated. The fight became a weekly ritual in a basement. Men came to watch, then to participate. Rules were declared. Silence outside the club. One fight at a time. No shirts, no shoes. The basement filled with clerks, mechanics, waiters, and executives desperate to become bruised and real.

Ada overdosed and called our house. Rex answered. He brought her back from the edge, then into his bed. Their affair shook the rotten walls night after night. I hated her voice, his laughter, and the way they excluded me.

Rex expanded his soap business. We stole bags of fat from a cosmetic surgery clinic, rendered them in the kitchen, poured the purified remains into moulds, and sold the bars back to department stores for eighty dollars each.

One afternoon, Rex kissed my hand and dusted it with lye. Pain bloomed white and absolute. I tried to escape into meditation, into imaginary caves and cool air, but he held me there.

“Stay,” he said. “This is happening.”

The scar became a mouth on my skin.

At work, I beat myself bloody in my manager’s office, hurled myself against shelves, then crawled toward him as security arrived. I told him what the evidence would look like. He agreed to pay me to stay away.

By then the club had become Havoc. Shaven recruits crowded the house, sleeping on floors, answering questions with rehearsed obedience. Rex gave orders. They smashed corporate windows, defaced advertisements, sabotaged monuments to credit and consumption.

Then Rex drove us into oncoming traffic. He released the wheel, smiling as horns screamed. The car rolled into darkness. I crawled from the wreck.

Rex disappeared.

When Ogden, one of Havoc’s members, was shot dead during an operation, the others spoke of him as if his death were promotion. I tried to shut everything down. No one listened.

I travelled from city to city and found identical basement clubs, identical rules, identical bruised faces. Everywhere, men greeted me with reverence.

“Mr. Marrow.”

The truth arrived slowly, then all at once. Rex wore my body. He acted while I slept. His absences were mine. His plans moved through my hands.

Ada confirmed it with exhausted contempt. There had never been another man in her bed. Only me.

Havoc’s final operation was already underway. The towers housing the debt-record companies had been mined. I entered one tower and searched for the charges, trying to undo what my sleeping self had built.

Rex found me in the stairwell. He beat me down flight after flight, though every blow landed on the same body. At the bottom, I understood that I could not kill him from outside.

I put the gun in my mouth.

Rex smiled.

I fired through my cheek.

He vanished.

The shaven recruits delivered Ada to the tower as if completing an order. She stared at the blood running down my neck, but she took my hand. Together we stood at the window.

Across the city, lights blinked in the debt towers. Then the buildings folded downward, floor into floor, while the glass trembled beneath our joined hands.

The cardiologist gave Aaron Vale weeks. His heart, once obedient enough to let him lose himself in equations, had become an exhausted muscle stuttering toward silence. Unless a donor appeared, he would die.

Della sat beside his bed, though they had lived apart for nearly a year. She spoke urgently about the sperm Aaron had frozen before his health collapsed. She wanted his consent to be inseminated before he died.

“A part of you could remain,” she said.

Aaron looked at the gray light in the window and wondered why survival, even imagined survival, felt like another demand.

Across the city, Wes Tarrow was trying to become a righteous man. Since leaving prison, he had found God, held down a job and begun coaching boys’ baseball. He prayed loudly, corrected strangers and treated every setback as a test sent personally by heaven. His wife, Nita, watched his faith harden into fanaticism. She knew the temper beneath it. Their children knew when to leave a room.

Lena Ward believed she had escaped the worst part of her own life. Once, she had measured days in cocaine and shame. Now she lived in a quiet suburb with Doug and their two young daughters. There were lunches to pack, baths to supervise, small shoes by the door. She mistook peace for permanence.

One afternoon, Wes’s pickup struck Doug and the girls in a crossing.

He kept driving. Then he braked, turned around and saw the broken shapes in the road. Terror seized him. He fled again.

At the hospital, Lena sat beneath fluorescent lights while a doctor told her that Doug and both children were dead. The words entered her one at a time and left nothing standing.

Doug’s heart went to Aaron.

When Aaron woke after the transplant, he drew a deep breath without pain. For the first time in months, he felt alive. Beneath the bandages, another man’s heart beat steadily, insistently, as if it had arrived carrying unfinished business.

Wes lasted two days before walking into a police station. He confessed to the hit-and-run and was sent back to prison. He called it God’s judgment. Nita called it abandonment.

Lena returned to cocaine. She did not relapse so much as enlist the drug in a methodical campaign against herself. She stopped answering calls, stopped eating, stopped caring whether morning came.

Aaron could not stop wondering about the heart inside him. Gratitude became curiosity, then obsession. He hired a private investigator, who gave him Doug’s name, the accident report and Lena’s address.

Aaron followed her. He watched her drift through days like a ghost. At a public swimming pool, he engineered a meeting, pretending chance had placed them beside the same blue water. Lena distrusted him, then wanted him, and soon they were sleeping together in borrowed rooms.

Della continued trying to conceive with Aaron’s frozen sperm. When Aaron left her, he said he did not want the child.

“You wanted to live,” she said. “Just not with me.”

Eventually he told Lena the truth.

“Doug’s heart is in me.”

She struck him, cursed him and threw him out. By morning she called him back. She pressed her ear to his chest and wept against the beat she recognized only because she needed to.

Wes was released early. Prison had stripped away his certainty. He went home long enough to tell Nita that he no longer believed, then walked out on her and the children. He found work at a distant motel, changing sheets and fixing drains beneath a false name.

Lena learned where he was. She told Aaron that Wes had to die. Her demand became the proof she required of his love.

Aaron bought a gun and tracked Wes to the motel. He confronted him behind the laundry building, but when Wes stood waiting, almost relieved, Aaron could not pull the trigger cleanly. The shot tore through Wes’s side.

“Run,” Aaron told him.

Aaron and Lena returned to their own motel. Later, bleeding through a makeshift bandage, Wes followed them and knocked on the door. He looked at Aaron with exhausted pleading.

“Finish it.”

Aaron raised the gun. Then he turned it against himself.

Lena screamed. Wes caught Aaron as he fell, and together they dragged him to the truck and drove him to the hospital. Doctors fought for the transplanted heart, but it failed inside Aaron’s ruined body.

Afterward, Wes went home to Nita and their children, carrying no scripture and making no promises.

Lena learned she was pregnant. She returned alone to the empty suburban house, where dust lay on the girls’ abandoned shoes. Inside her, a new heart had begun its small, secret beating.

Solly Two Coats robbed the diamond house in a northern port dressed like a man bound for heaven. His crew wore pilgrim grey, carried prayer books, and murmured blessings while guards bowed them through the doors. They walked out just as solemnly, with a stone in Solly’s case big enough to buy forgiveness for every sin they had committed.

His cousin Marv called from overseas.

“Bring it straight over,” Marv said.

Before Solly sailed, Grigor the Nail found him at the docks and recommended a bookmaker’s in the city, a place where a man could wager heavily without questions. At the same time, Grigor whispered to the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that Solly would be there carrying something worth stealing.

Elsewhere, the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. Sam mistook contempt for charm and tried to force the price down. A bare-knuckle fighter named Finn objected. One punch left Sam senseless in the mud.

That presented Halloway with a difficulty. Sam had been promised for a fixed bout arranged by the gang boss Coldstone. With Sam unable to stand, Halloway put Finn in his place.

“He goes down in the fourth,” Coldstone said.

“In the fourth,” Halloway promised.

Solly arrived in the city, delivered the diamond to the fence Hersch, then carried his case to Grigor’s bookmaker’s and laid money on the fight. Ike and Benno came through the back with Tulley, a nervous accomplice who brought along his dog. Their robbery collapsed almost immediately. They seized Solly’s case and, when he would not release it, took his arm with it. Grigor appeared shooting and chased them into the street.

That evening, Finn entered the ring knowing nothing of arrangements. In the first round he struck his opponent once, cleanly, and the man fell cold.

Coldstone lost a fortune. Halloway lost several teeth.

All night the helicopters crossed the city, their lights sliding over roofs and swimming pools, hospitals and bakeries, clubs and darkened schoolyards. They sprayed for crop pests, though there were no crops in sight, only neighbourhood after neighbourhood settling beneath the chemical mist.

Doctor Neil Hartigan buttoned his shirt while his wife, Bess, stood before a canvas in her dinner dress, adding one last stroke of blue. Their guests would arrive soon. Neil asked if she meant to wash the paint from her hands. Bess said she liked it there.

Across town, Otto Kemp wrote HAPPY BIRTHDAY CHARLIE on an order slip. Charlie Rill’s mother promised to collect the cake after school.

Charlie never reached school. He stepped from the curb, and Rhona, a waitress hurrying to work, struck him with her car. He rose before anyone could stop him and walked home, repeating that he was fine. At home he lay down, closed his eyes, and could not be wakened.

Grant and Elaine kept vigil beside their son’s hospital bed. Machines breathed and blinked around him. Grant’s estranged father, Duff, appeared carrying an old coat and an older grievance. He sat without being invited and confessed that, decades before, he had slept with another woman. Grant stared at him as if this were one more emergency for which no doctor had been called.

The cake remained at Otto’s bakery. Unpaid and ignored, he telephoned the Rills anonymously. At first he asked why they had forgotten. Then his voice hardened. He called again and again, leaving threats beneath the ringing.

In another living room, Cheryl spoke softly into a telephone, guiding unseen men through fantasies while her husband, Stu, sat beside her, jaw clenched. Each intimate word seemed directed at everyone but him.

Stu escaped with three friends on a fishing trip. At the river they found a young woman floating face down, pale hair stirring in the current. They tethered her wrist to the bank so she would not drift away, then opened their beers and fished. For two days they cast their lines past her body before telling anyone.

When Vern came home, his wife Iris was removing her party-clown makeup. He told her what they had done. The painted smile remained while the woman beneath it recoiled.

Every night Vida sang beneath club lights, bending heartbreak into melody. At home her daughter Bee drew a bow across her cello and listened to the empty rooms answer.

Officer Rowe told his wife, Peg, one lie and his lover, Nan, another. When the family dog threatened to expose where he had been, he drove it away and abandoned it. Nan’s former husband, Cass, a helicopter pilot, discovered that she had a new man. He entered her house with a saw and reduced chairs, tables, and cabinets to jagged halves.

While the Hartigans were out, Ike and Dot house-sat for them. Dot painted bruises onto her face and lay twisted on the floor. Ike photographed her as though documenting a murder.

At the Hartigans’ dinner party, wine loosened what courtesy had restrained. Bess admitted that years ago she had posed nude for an artist, and that there had been an affair. Neil made a scene, demanding details in front of everyone while Bess sat with blue paint still beneath her nails.

Charlie died before morning.

Grant and Elaine finally traced the menacing calls to Otto’s bakery. They arrived ready for rage, but Otto saw their faces and understood. He brought out warm bread. They ate together in the bakery’s heat, and Otto grieved with them for the boy whose cake would never be collected.

Bee came home and found Vida asleep. She looked at her mother, then closed the garage door. She sat in the car with the engine running until the cello, waiting inside, seemed very far away.

Later, at a picnic in the hills, Stu watched a young woman move against the bright sky. Something in him broke loose. He lifted a rock and smashed it into her head.

That evening a tremor passed beneath the whole city. Glass rattled, pictures tilted, hospital lights flickered, and the river shivered in its banks. Then the newsreader appeared, composed beneath studio lights, and folded every death, every wreck, every private catastrophe into a single evening bulletin.

At the party in Emlyn’s house, Wilder waited until the rooms downstairs had become loud with drink. Then he touched Odile’s elbow and led her up the narrow staircase, past the bedroom where the coats had been thrown, into a little room overlooking the dark garden.

“You are very lovely,” he told her.

Below them, someone dropped a glass and everyone cheered. Odile stood close enough for him to smell smoke in her hair.

They rented two rooms in a quiet district where no one knew them. At first there was only a bed and a chair, but gradually they bought linen, plates, cups, a kettle, and a blue bowl for fruit. Their affair acquired cupboards and washing-up. Wilder brought books from publishers’ offices; Odile brought flowers and once a small lamp. It seemed to them that they had made a household outside the world.

Then Odile told him she was carrying Emlyn’s child.

They sat on the edge of the bed, looking at the blue bowl on the table. Wilder asked what they were to do.

“Exactly what we have been doing,” she said.

So the rooms went on exactly as before.

Months later, in a hotel abroad, Emlyn paused at the desk while Odile looked through a guidebook. The clerk produced a letter held for her. Emlyn saw the handwriting before she could take it.

“Wilder?” he asked.

Upstairs, with the shutters closed against the afternoon glare, Odile confessed. She told him about the party, the rooms, the linen and plates, and all the hours she had removed from their marriage.

Emlyn listened without interruption.

When she had finished, he said, “The curious thing is, I have always been fonder of him than of you.”

On their return, Odile went to the rented rooms at the customary hour. Wilder was there with wine and sandwiches. She said nothing whatever about the hotel, the letter, or her confession. They ate, went to bed, and washed the glasses afterward. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had.

Soon after, Emlyn invited Wilder to lunch. They remained in the restaurant for hours while Emlyn drank steadily and attacked contemporary fiction with bright, elaborate contempt.

“You agents have abolished the sentence,” he said. “In return, you’ve given us the sensitive young man in a bedsitting room.”

Wilder defended authors he disliked and praised novels he had not finished. Emlyn baited him until coffee, ordered brandy, and began again. He never once mentioned what he knew.

At dinner in the married couple’s house, the two men were easier with each other. They discussed racquet games, then schoolboy sport: wet fields, cruel masters, the proper grip, the old humiliations of changing rooms. Odile tried twice to enter the conversation. Neither attempt survived. By dessert, she had no part in the talk at all.

The rented rooms lost their charm. The linen needed replacing; the kettle leaked; dust gathered on the books Wilder had meant to remove. What had once seemed a second life became an appointment and then a chore. They divided the crockery without quarrelling. Odile took the blue bowl. Wilder dealt with the landlord and surrendered the lease.

Two years later they met by chance in a bar. Odile looked older, though perhaps it was only the harsh light.

“My marriage is over,” she said.

Wilder put down his drink.

“I spent all last night telling Emlyn everything.”

“Everything?”

“The rooms. The years. You.”

In the strained talk that followed, she let slip that Emlyn had been publishing Peller, a novelist Wilder represented. Both men privately considered Peller vain, fraudulent, and almost unreadable. Yet Emlyn had kept bringing out his books.

Wilder’s face altered.

He went home and telephoned Emlyn in a state. Emlyn arrived that evening, calm and faintly annoyed, as if summoned over a disputed royalty statement.

“How long?” Wilder demanded.

Emlyn accepted a drink but did not touch it.

“Four years. Odile told me abroad.”

Wilder stared at him. “But the lunches. Your house. Peller.”

“Yes.”

“And my letters?”

Emlyn finally smiled.

“I recognised the hand at the hotel,” he said. “Though, if it comforts you, I never thought much of your letters either.”

He was born in a small industrial town where chimneys darkened the snow and factory whistles divided each day into shifts. From the beginning he seemed ill-suited to the place: narrow-shouldered, weak-eyed, given to long silences and peculiar questions.

His father tried to cure him of timidity by throwing him into the deep end of the municipal pool. The boy sank without struggle. From the tiles below, he watched the shattered silver of the surface until someone hauled him out. For years afterward, he remembered the bottom as peaceful.

The army conscripted him and made him a chaplain’s assistant, though he had scarcely been trained to salute, much less survive a war. Overseas, during a retreat, he became lost behind the lines with a scout whose boots were splitting and whose temper was worse. When the boy asked to be left in the snow to die, the scout struck him until he stood again.

They were captured soon afterward. On the prison train, packed among coughing men, the scout’s wounded foot blackened with gangrene. He died during the journey, staring at the boy and blaming him with his last breath for every wrong turn and wasted hour.

The surviving prisoner was taken to a camp where enemy officers lived strangely well. A clerical error had granted them double rations for years, and no one had corrected it. They traded the surplus for soap, tobacco, blankets, and the appearance of civilization. He watched them pour cream into tea while men beyond the wire scraped frost from boards.

Later he was sent to a great city, almost untouched by the war. He and other prisoners were housed in a disused abattoir, sleeping below ground in a meat locker whose hooks still hung from the ceiling.

One night, fire came from the sky.

The prisoners heard the city roaring above them while the insulated chamber remained cool and dark. In the morning they climbed out and found streets turned to ash, roofs melted away, and whole neighborhoods erased. The city had become a smoking plain.

They were made to dig into cellars for bodies. Some lay curled like sleepers; others crumbled when touched. The work continued until one of the diggers began retching. Nothing came up. He heaved and heaved, dry as the ruins, then fell dead among them.

Another prisoner, who had loved the dead scout, whispered that the weak-eyed boy was responsible. “Not here,” he promised. “Not yet. But one day I’ll have you killed.”

After the war, the boy came home a man in years only. He collapsed and was hospitalized. A patient in the neighboring bed introduced him to the books of a hack science fiction writer whose paperbacks were full of time traps, distant planets, and machines that misunderstood their makers. The stories seemed less fantastic to him than ordinary life.

He married the daughter of the owner of an optometry school. He became an optometrist, then a prosperous one, then a rich man with employees, investments, and a large house where no room felt entirely real.

Years later, he survived an air crash in the mountains. While he lay injured, his wife drove frantically toward the hospital. A damaged exhaust system filled her car with fumes. She arrived unconscious and died before she could see him.

After that, he began speaking of aliens.

They had taken him, he said, to their planet and displayed him in a zoo with a film actress. The enclosure looked like a furnished home, but unseen crowds watched them. The aliens explained that every moment existed at once. Birth, death, love, fire, and silence were permanent features of the universe. Free will, they said, was an idea peculiar to Earth.

He went on a late-night radio program and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. Callers laughed. The host asked whether grief was real if the dead remained alive elsewhere in time.

His daughter heard the broadcast and decided he was senile. She took his accounts, his appointments, and his business affairs out of his hands. He did not resist. He said she had always done so and always would.

He also said he knew how he would die.

After addressing a crowd about the permanence of all moments, he paused beneath the lights. Somewhere beyond the stage stood an old enemy fulfilling an old promise. A beam weapon flashed.

He fell dead exactly when, where, and how he had always known he would.

And elsewhere, forever, a peculiar boy rested peacefully at the bottom of a pool, looking up at the light.
